**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

alias tells contains_eager which FROM object to search for in the eager load but does not participate in building up the "path", and in this case you also need [of_type()](http://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/latest/orm/inheritance_loading.html?highlight=of_type#eager-loading-of-specific-or-polymorphic-subtypes) to build the path correctly (need to fix some of the of_type() links)



```
abc = Query(A1) \
    .outerjoin(B1, A1.b).options(contains_eager(A1.b.of_type(B1))) \
    .outerjoin(C1, B1.c1).options(contains_eager(A1.b.of_type(B1), B1.c1.of_type(C1)))
print(abc)

```


```
SELECT b.a_id AS b_a_id, b.type AS b_type, b.id AS b_id, c.b_id AS c_b_id, c.type AS c_type, c.id AS c_id, a.type AS a_type, a.id AS a_id 
FROM a LEFT OUTER JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id AND b.type IN (:type_1) LEFT OUTER JOIN c ON b.id = c.b_id AND c.type IN (:type_2) 
WHERE a.type IN (:type_3)

```


the use of "alias" seems like it shouldn't be needed here but at the moment it is needed.

There's some docs that could be improved here but at the moment nothing I want to do with contains_eager().

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

Well, OK, this one is weird.  But yes I think when you send the path to contains_eager(), the element you put into "of_type()" in this context has to be de-aliased, but you can still use the alias everywhere else:

```
A_A1 = aliased(A1, name='aaa')
A_B1 = aliased(B1, name='bbb')
A_C1 = aliased(C1, name='ccc')

abc = Query(A1) \
    .outerjoin(A_B1, A1.b).options(
        contains_eager(A1.b.of_type(B1), alias=A_B1)) \
    .outerjoin(C1, A_B1.c1).options(
        contains_eager(
            A1.b.of_type(B1), B1.c1.of_type(C1), alias=A_C1))
print(abc)

```

as far as how to "de-alias" something, sure, that can work like this:


```
A1 = aliased(A1, name='aaa')
B1 = aliased(B1, name='bbb')
C1 = aliased(C1, name='ccc')

abc = Query(A1) \
    .outerjoin(B1, A1.b).options(
        contains_eager(A1.b.of_type(inspect(B1).mapper), alias=B1)) \
    .outerjoin(C1, B1.c1).options(
        contains_eager(
            A1.b.of_type(inspect(B1).mapper), B1.c1.of_type(inspect(C1).mapper), alias=C1))

```

now, the question is, can/should contains_eager (and other options) do this for you automatically?   plus send the "alias" argument automatically when you have of_type().  I think the answer is yes but I need to dig into this to make sure...e.g. when is it ever valid to have an "alias" inside of of_type() when you're in a mapper option?   .   But for now, you can build a helper function for yourself to do that contains_eager() boilerplate.     I think I can make it automatic but this might be a longer release cycle, may be a 1.2 thing, not sure, need to try it out.

**Michael Bayer ([@zzzeek](https://github.com/zzzeek)) wrote:**

Intercept contains_eager() with of_type, set aliased / polymorphic

Fixed bug in :func:`.contains_eager` query option where making use of a
path that used :meth:`.PropComparator.of_type` to refer to a subclass
across more than one level of joins would also require that the "alias"
argument were provided with the same subtype in order to avoid adding
unwanted FROM clauses to the query; additionally,  using
:func:`.contains_eager` across subclasses that use :func:`.aliased` objects
of subclasses as the :meth:`.PropComparator.of_type` argument will also
render correctly.

Change-Id: Ie1c10924faa45251aab1a076a3ba7ef9fb1bdeee
Fixes: #4130
